clue.text: Poor whiskey strained

parts.note: W is Whiskey in the NATO phonetic alphabet
retched means heaved or strained to vomit

explanation.surface: A drinker complains that the whiskey they were served had been badly strained.
explanation.definitionFit: Wretched describes someone miserable or unfortunate, a synonym of poor in the pitying sense.

clue.text: Little island that could stun the world?

parts.note: to rock is to shock or stun
all is everything, the whole world

explanation.surface: A tiny island with enough force to shake the whole planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Rockall is a tiny uninhabited islet in the North Atlantic, a familiar name from the shipping forecast.

clue.text: Had nice duty to broadcast, as historian

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, so the letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A historian felt it a pleasant obligation to go on air.
explanation.definitionFit: Thucydidean means in the manner of Thucydides, the ancient Greek historian of the Peloponnesian War.

clue.text: One that can't stand half-hearted party host

indicators.note: the doubled letter at the heart loses one of its pair, half of the middle

parts.note: the Mad Hatter hosts the tea party in Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: A grumpy party host shows no enthusiasm for the guests.
explanation.definitionFit: A hater detests something, someone who cannot stand it or bear it.

clue.text: Paper towel covers tramp

indicators.note: the towel word covers the paper word, wrapping round it

parts.note: a towel is a drier of wet things
FT is the Financial Times

explanation.surface: A homeless person wraps a newspaper in a towel for warmth.
explanation.definitionFit: A drifter is a vagrant who wanders without settling, a synonym for tramp.

clue.text: Bachelor, one savouring of scandal — but not this crime?

parts.note: gamy (or gamey) means racy or suggestive of scandal

explanation.surface: A single man with a taste for gossip is cleared of one particular offence.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark carries the joke: a bachelor, being unmarried, is the one person who cannot commit this crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigamy, marrying while already married, is a criminal offence, the crime pointed to.

clue.text: Rears footballers, entertaining team

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one word holds the other

parts.note: backs are defensive players
a side is a team

explanation.surface: Defenders put on a show for their own team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rears' looks like a verb, as in rearing children; it is the plural noun for bottoms.
explanation.definitionFit: Backsides and rears are both informal words for the buttocks.

clue.text: It fixes stage up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or race

explanation.surface: Something used to hold scenery in place on a theatre stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Gel, like hair gel, sets and holds things in place, so it is a fixative.

clue.text: Offa for one was stirring cream in

indicators.note: stirring mixes things around, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone named Offa was busy stirring cream into a bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: Offa was an eighth-century king of Mercia, the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Offa ruled the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia, so he is an example of a Mercian.

clue.text: Unconvincing sort of reasoning by judges in official bulletin

parts.note: a court is the judges sitting collectively
circular reasoning assumes what it sets out to prove

explanation.surface: A newspaper item criticises judges for flimsy logic in a formal announcement.
explanation.walkthrough: The Court Circular is the daily published record of the British royal family's engagements.
explanation.definitionFit: The Court Circular is the official daily record of royal engagements published in British newspapers.

clue.text: Tom informally watched you

parts.note: saw is the past tense of see, to watch
yer is an informal spoken form of you, as the word informally signals

explanation.surface: Someone tells a man called Tom, in casual speech, that they spotted him.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Sawyer is the boy hero of Mark Twain's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Sawyer is Mark Twain's famous fictional boy, so the surname completes the name given.

clue.text: State's job not finished with excessive enthusiasm

indicators.note: a job not finished lacks its final part, so the last letter of the word is lopped

parts.note: a task is a job of work
a mania is a craze or obsessive enthusiasm

explanation.surface: A report says some task was left incomplete because of overzealous workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasmania is an island state of Australia, so it is an example of a state.

clue.text: Steal from the Prado? Not a Goya, certainly

parts.note: to abstract is to remove or purloin
the Prado museum in Madrid holds art

explanation.surface: A thief takes a picture from the Madrid gallery, but it is no Goya.
explanation.definitionFit: Goya painted figurative scenes, so non-representational abstract work is certainly not one of his.

clue.text: Shut up in one way before being put in the earth

indicators.note: these letters are placed inside the word for a lump of earth

parts.note: a clod is a lump of earth
ST is short for street
ere is a poetic word for before

explanation.surface: Instructions for a burial: one route taken before the body goes into the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloistered means secluded as in a monastery, an adjectival sense of shut up or confined.

clue.text: Extra for mortgage raised in review of platoon

indicators.note: the raised word sits inside the rearranged letters
a review revises and reorders, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
raised means up

explanation.surface: A soldier seeks more home loan cash at a parade inspection.
explanation.definitionFit: A top-up loan is additional borrowing added to an existing mortgage.

clue.text: To swim said to be the alternative to this depression

definitions.text: To swim said to be the alternative to this
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the saying ... or swim pairs this word with swim
second meaning: a hollow or basin in the ground, or a kitchen basin

explanation.walkthrough: The first half points to the stock phrase sink or swim; the second is a plain hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: A sink is a basin or hollow, and it is also the grim option offered against swimming in the proverb.

clue.text: Foreign priest moves infant's head back

indicators.note: the word's leading letter is shifted to a new place within it
the first letter goes back one place, behind its neighbour

parts.note: a babe is an infant; the apostrophe-s is just possessive surface

explanation.surface: A priest abroad gently tilts a baby's head backwards, perhaps at a christening.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbé is a French cleric, so this is a priest from abroad.

clue.text: Delivery for doorman

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a short-pitched ball in cricket that rears up at the batsman
second meaning: a ... guards the door of a club

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a bouncer is a fast ball pitched short so it rises sharply towards the batter.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a hostile cricket ball and a nightclub's door security man.

clue.text: Said "Repent!" to reform street walker

indicators.note: to reform is to reshape, so the letters are formed again in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A preacher urges a streetwalker to repent and change her ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Street walker' suggests a prostitute; read literally it is simply someone walking in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestrian is literally someone who travels on foot through the streets.

clue.text: Day-long, reeds regularly dropped into the sea

parts.note: to long for something is to itch for it

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals, every second one

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the word are the ones kept

explanation.surface: Reeds were thrown into the water during a long day of clearing.
explanation.definitionFit: To ditch an aircraft is to bring it down in the sea, an emergency landing on water.

clue.text: Colleague in gold rush at first an enthusiast

indicators.note: the colleague sits inside the gold symbol

parts.note: a mate is a work colleague

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the word rush

explanation.surface: A partner in a gold rush began as a keen hobbyist prospector.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur does something for love rather than money, a devotee or enthusiast.

clue.text: Kitchen worker's opportunity to return pieces of advice

parts.note: your turn is your chance or opportunity

indicators.note: to return here is to come back, so the word runs in the opposite direction

parts.note: tips are helpful hints

explanation.surface: A cook gets the chance to pass back some kitchen hints.
explanation.definitionFit: A turnspit was a servant, or a dog, whose job was to turn meat roasting on a spit.

clue.text: German book by an author from Scotland

parts.note: Buch is German for book
taken as written

explanation.surface: A German volume sits beside a work by a Scottish writer.
explanation.definitionFit: John Buchan, author of The Thirty-Nine Steps, was a Scottish novelist.

clue.text: Lack of a taxi upset philosopher

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the words upside down, reading them backwards

parts.note: no means none, a lack
a cab is a taxi

explanation.surface: A thinker gets cross when no cab turns up.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon was an English philosopher and statesman of the scientific method.

clue.text: Foolishly touches the cat: take out the flannel

indicators.note: done foolishly, the letters are rearranged without sense

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone foolishly strokes the cat and is told to stop the waffle.
explanation.walkthrough: Flannel is British slang for evasive talk or waffle.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut to the chase is to drop the waffle and get to the point.

clue.text: Short skirt brings disapproving expression

indicators.note: a short version lacks its final letter

parts.note: a tutu is a ballet skirt

explanation.surface: A very brief skirt earns tutting from onlookers.
explanation.definitionFit: Tut is the clicking exclamation people make to show disapproval.

clue.text: A crust to eat — old woman digests it, on reflection

indicators.note: a word that digests another holds it inside, as food in the stomach

parts.note: gran is a grandmother

indicators.note: a reflection shows a mirror image, so the two letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Grandma polishes off a crusty dish and thinks about it afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A gratin is a browned crust of breadcrumbs or cheese on a dish, or the dish itself.

clue.text: Change properties of article, clamping set of teeth round

indicators.note: teeth clamp on what they hold, so one word grips the other
the set of teeth goes round the article, enclosing it

parts.note: a denture is a set of false teeth
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A dentist adjusts a denture by clamping it round some item.
explanation.definitionFit: To denature is to alter the natural properties of a substance, such as a protein or alcohol.
